sweep_summary: Three works with stress in the title, all by Larry Hagberg and all already listed. (1) Hagberg 1988 'Stress and length in Mayo' (Shipley ed., In Honor of Mary Haas, pp. 361-376; DOI 10.1515/9783110852387.361) is paywalled at De Gruyter (JS bot-wall) and the archive.org copy is a lending-restricted scan; via the archive.org full-text-search API I recovered highlight snippets (two phonological classes of free forms, 'non-mobile' vs 'mobile' stress, stress and length as a function of position in the phrase; the 1986 conference abstract in SIL Notes on Linguistics 38 p. 44 says the same) — snippet-level, consistent with the catalog's lexical coding; medium priority to read in full. (2) Hagberg 1989b 'Floating accent in Mayo' (Arizona Phonology Conference 2 / Coyote Papers, pp. 32-47) could not be obtained: repository.arizona.edu could not be reached by automated download, no archive.org/OpenAlex/Google Books copy; its content is superseded by the dissertation's sec. 5.1 of the same title, so low priority. (3) The dissertation (Hagberg 1993, SIL e-book 2006) was downloaded open from archive.org (PDF 365 pp. + text; MPI handle could not be reached by automated download) and read: sec. 3.1.1.2 pp. 139-152 and ch. 5 pp. 233-315 confirm the catalog's 'lexical' coding — one stress (high pitch) on the first or second syllable of the word, lexically fixed per stem (~50/50), stable under prefixation, weight-insensitive, second-syllable stress the default, with phrase-final length/stress interactions. The catalog quote is verbatim on pp. 140-141; the fuller passage (adding 'no way to predict.. must somehow be marked in the lexicon') is the best statement read and does not supersede the catalog source since it is the same work. Bonus find in the same 1988 volume: Burnham 1988 'Mayo suprasegmentals' (Jijiri/Navojoa Mayo: accent usually on the first syllable, otherwise the second; Escalante's count roughly two-to-one first-syllable) — snippet-only, refines the frequency claim, medium priority. Held held by the project and re-checked for context: Freeze 1989 (Mayo de Los Capomos, Sinaloa; our earlier reading) states a penultimate default with shape-conditioned classes (CV:CV final stress, CVCV(C) initial stress) for that dialect — a different variety, not a works with stress in the title. No remained; and updated in the mayo1264 our files.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the same text (1993 dissertation, reissued by SIL 2006 as 'a slightly revised version' per the SIL editor's note in the PuRe record) that the existing_statements entry already quotes from pp. 140-141; the reading matches the existing statement exactly (single stress on syllable 1 or 2, lexically determined, no secondary stress, weight irrelevant, phrase-final leftward shift in disyllables). The catalog_records entry has an empty rule string; this source fills it as lexical first-or-second-syllable stress. Nothing new beyond the existing statement except the explicit page for the phrase-final shift (pp. 276-277) and the formal rule (14) on p. 144.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every word carries exactly one stress (realized as high pitch), on either its first or its second syllable counted from the left edge of the whole word, prefixes included; which of the two a stem takes is unpredictable from phonology or morphology and is a lexical property of the stem (about half the lexicon each; Hagberg analyses second-syllable stress as the default, built by a single left-to-right syllabic foot with right-linked stress, and first-syllable stress as a lexical accent). Coda consonants (syllable weight) play no role for short-vowel words. Formal statement (14), p. 144: build a single syllabic foot from left to right; insert * in the foot and link from right to left. Phrase-final position modifies this: an unaccented (second-syllable-stressed) disyllable shifts its stress to the first syllable and lengthens that vowel when the word ends a phrase (Phrase-Final Extrametricality, pp. 276-277), but words of three or more syllables do not shift.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: 'there is no secondary stress' (p. 140; repeated p. 234).
new_statements.exceptions: Words with vowel length are deferred to sec. 5.2 ('the distribution of stress is not so easily stated for words containing long vowels', fn. 7, p. 141); derived vowel length correlates with second-syllable stress and derived consonant gemination with first-syllable stress (p. 143). Phrase-final disyllables with underlying second-syllable stress surface with first-syllable stress plus lengthening (pp. 276-277); no shift in words of three or more syllables. Monosyllables before a stressed syllable show lower pitch (phrase-level downdrift, fn. 6, p. 140). Stress is stable under prefixation (hi-, hihi-): the stem's pattern is kept, with stress on the prefix when the stem is first-syllable-accented.
new_statements.identity_note: Hagberg's data are from his own SIL field notes gathered 1983-1990 'in a number of villages of the Mayo River valley and Fuerte River valley' (p. 139, repeated p. 233), i.e. both the Sonoran (Río Mayo) and Sinaloan (Río Fuerte) Mayo areas, supplemented by Collard & Collard 1962; no single village dialect is named as the basis. The SIL 2006 e-book is a slightly revised reissue of the 1993 University of Arizona dissertation; the copy read is the 1993 UMI edition (archive.org), not the 2006 SIL PDF, which is could not be reached by automated download.

new_statements.relation_note: Same author and same analysis as the existing statement from Hagberg 1993 (diss.) sec. 3.1.1.2: single culminative stress on syllable 1 or 2 from the left word edge, lexically determined (about half the lexicon each per Collard & Collard 1962), second-syllable stress unmarked, first-syllable stress = lexical (floating) accent, no secondary stress, high pitch as the cue, phrase-final leftward shift. The 1989 paper is the earlier conference version; it adds nothing that changes the placement, only the compound-word secondary-stress remark (n. 1) and the explicit H&V rule set (14). The catalog record itself has an empty rule field; this source supports the 'lexical' coding carried by the exist…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every Mayo word carries exactly one stress (realized as high pitch), on either the first or the second syllable counted from the left edge of the word, prefixes included; which of the two is a lexical property of the stem: unaccented stems (the unmarked class, about half the lexicon and nearly all Spanish loans) get second-syllable stress by rule (14) (bounded right-headed feet built left to right, left-headed word tree, conflation), while accented stems carry a floating lexical accent [H] that docks on the leftmost vowel of the word (so stress stays word-initial even when prefixes such as reduplicative or xi- are added) and forces a degenerate initial foot, giving first-syllable stress. Syllable weight plays no role in placement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None in simple words ('there is no secondary stress, except in compound words', p. 33; rule (14c) conflation = 'only one stress is assigned per word', n. 3 p. 45); n. 1 p. 45: secondary stress, confined to compounds, is impressionistically a pitch level intermediate between high and low.
new_statements.exceptions: n. 2 p. 45: 'Mayo has phrase-final extrametricality which forces stress to shift to the preceding syllable when it would otherwise occur phrase-finally. Any analysis of Mayo stress that is based on a word list will therefore be misleading.' Loanwords: 'with very few exceptions' borrowed words take second-syllable stress (p. 35). Stress assignment is cyclic and the accent refloats after reduplication (sec. 2, pp. 37-42).
new_statements.identity_note: Hagberg's data are Mayo of Sonora (his SIL fieldwork; the 1986 Haas Festival abstract is titled 'Stress and length in Mayo of Sonora'); the 1989 paper itself just says 'Mayo, a Uto-Aztecan language of northwestern Mexico' and notes the two reduplicative prefixes differ in meaning in closely related Yaqui but not in Mayo.

tone_statements.quote: The above constraint asserts that high tone, which is the sole distinguishing feature of Mayo stress, cannot be associated to the second mora of a syllable. (24) Accent: Left-Anchor: Foot – H The above constraint says that a high tone (i.e., stress) goes on the left edge of a foot. I have assigned the label Accent to this constraint because it produces the effect (when unviolated) of exceptional initial stress. Thus, this constraint is relevant only to those inputs which are lexically marked for it ... [note 3:] The sole phonetic feature of stress is high pitch. The lexicon is fairly evenly divided between words with first syllable stress and words with second syllable stress.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: every clause of the deciding quotation and the loanword-default excerpt is verbatim in the held archive.org text of Hagberg 1993 at the stated sections/pages (pp. 140-141, 150-151, fn. 7). Deciding source: a 1993 phonology dissertation by the SIL field linguist of Mayo, based on seven years of his own field data, a 1600-item lexical survey and an instrumental pilot (Hagberg 1988b); Glottolog lists no phonology monograph, no JIPA illustration and only one print grammar (de Wolf 1997, Spanish), so this is the best available stress description and it is. The second held source, Freeze 1989 (Capomos/Sinaloa dialect, provisional), frames stress as penult-default with shape-conditioned exceptions, but its CV:CV->sigma2 and CVCV+gemination->sigma1 facts match Hagberg's length/stress correlations, so it corroborates rather than contradicts the lexical sigma1-vs-sigma2 cod

sources.note: Jijiri (Navojoa, Sonora) Mayo: accent on the first syllable of the word in most words, otherwise on the second; interacts with vowel length and phrase-level tone; compares with Yaqui and reconstructs Proto-Sonoran initial accent. Agrees with the catalog's first-or-second-syllable lexical two-way split but gives a different frequency (first-syllable dominant, 'roughly two to one' per Escalante) from Hagberg's 'roughly evenly divided'. Snippet-level only.
